title: Multi-year, near-closed human life support for deep space

concept.text: The proposed innovation is an integrated life-support system that keeps a crew alive and healthy for years in deep space while requiring very little material from outside the habitat. It would recover and reuse essential materials, maintain a habitable environment, and support maintenance and recovery from failures throughout the mission. NASA’s account of International Space Station technology describes relevant air and water recycling and connects those capabilities to the goal of closed-loop systems for Mars; it does not establish that this broader capability has been achieved.

Proposed engineering scope: the system would integrate air, water, food and waste processing with contaminant control, nutrition, repair and fault recovery. Near-closure would mean keeping external material inputs and depletion of stored supplies within explicitly defined limits, rather than assuming that every material is recycled perfectly. Food, nutrients, consumables and replacement hardware would each need accounting. This scope is an engineering synthesis; the supplied source documents only part of it.

significance.text: If achieved with dependable maintenance and fault recovery, this capability would substantially reduce a central constraint on long voyages and remote habitation: the need to transport replacement supplies from Earth. NASA’s discussion connects recycling to missions where resupply is unavailable and describes limited cargo capacity and delays in obtaining additional supplies. The direct consequence of the proposed advance would be longer crewed operations with less dependence on repeated deliveries; its revolutionary significance is an inference from overcoming that logistical constraint.

Conditional downstream possibilities include more autonomous deep-space expeditions and outposts that can remain occupied through long gaps between deliveries. Permanent settlement would still depend on other capabilities, including protection of human health, radiation protection, dependable energy and suitable transportation. As a conceptual limit, material recycling does not imply energy independence or indefinite self-sufficiency: a habitat could recycle water efficiently while exhausting food, processing chemicals or spare parts. These are implications and boundaries of the proposed concept, rather than outcomes demonstrated by the supplied evidence.

missing_breakthrough.text: The target capability is sustained performance of the whole inhabited system over multiple years, including its response to degradation and failures. NASA documents air and water processing, trace-contaminant control and maintenance needs, providing relevant foundations. Those foundations do not establish that food supply, nutrient recovery, waste processing and replacement hardware can all be managed within a sufficiently small external-input budget.

Proposed engineering barriers include keeping coupled material flows balanced as crew demand and equipment performance change; maintaining safe water and air quality without allowing contaminants to accumulate; and managing food, nutrients and waste without exhausting essential inventories. The integration problem is consequential: material recovered by one process must be usable by the next, and losses that appear small over a short test may consume substantial reserves over several years. The supplied review does not establish a demonstrated solution to this full set of requirements or prescribe a particular biological or physicochemical architecture.

A further proposed barrier is maintaining the system within its own resource limits. Repairs consume parts, tools, processing materials, energy and crew time; replacement manufacturing would itself require feedstock and equipment. A convincing design therefore needs to account for recovery from realistic failures alongside routine recycling. The unresolved engineering question is whether these combined demands can remain within a practical mission budget, rather than whether an individual recycling device can operate efficiently.

current_state.text: The International Space Station recycles air and water while remaining dependent on resupply. A NASA article dated December 10, 2025, in the retained version marked updated May 4, 2026, reports that station systems can recover around 98% of the water brought to the station. The denominator matters: this is a water-recovery figure, not a percentage for total life-support closure, food production, nutrient recovery or hardware replacement. The supplied copy does not establish whether that precise wording was present in the article’s original December version.

The same NASA account describes air revitalization, oxygen generation, trace-contaminant removal, and maintenance and manufacturing work relevant to more autonomous exploration. It presents closed-loop systems for Mars as a goal informed by station experience. These are relevant subsystem capabilities and supporting technologies; the article does not report an integrated, multi-year crew demonstration covering the proposed food, nutrient, consumable and replacement-hardware budgets.

Evidence boundary: the supplied review describes the retained NASA article as identity-verified, complete and untruncated, and the source index reports no extraction issues. Interpretation is therefore not limited by a known missing portion of that article. However, the supplied bounded search record is empty, so the material does not establish a comprehensive picture of capabilities through the intended November 1, 2026 cutoff. It supports the dated NASA account, while leaving later developments and demonstrations elsewhere unresolved. That coverage limitation does not show that unreviewed results are false or prove that the broader capability remains unachieved.

completion_criteria.text: Proposed demonstration: a representative crew completes a multi-year inhabited test with independently measured material balances for water, oxygen, nutrients, food, consumables and replacement hardware. Before the test, investigators should specify the crew and duration, system boundary, initial inventories, permitted external inputs and maximum inventory depletion. All deliveries and replacement items should be included. These are proposed assessment criteria, not established standards or requirements prescribed by the supplied NASA article.
completion_criteria.label: Multi-year inhabited test independently accounts for full material balances

completion_criteria.text: The test should demonstrate sustained environmental quality and nutrition, alongside repair of realistic equipment failures within predefined budgets for parts, materials, energy and crew effort. Material accounting should reveal whether apparent closure depends on drawing down stored supplies. Independent scrutiny of measurements and methods, followed by repeat demonstrations, would strengthen confidence that the result is reproducible and applicable beyond a single favorable run.
completion_criteria.label: Sustained environmental quality and nutrition with budgeted equipment repairs

completion_criteria.text: A later deep-space demonstration should establish performance under the environmental and operational conditions actually encountered, including the tested restrictions on resupply and outside assistance. Its conclusions should remain bounded by crew size, duration, power availability, maintenance demands and the failures exercised. Finite tests can establish demonstrated breadth and reliability within those conditions; they cannot establish indefinite operation or successful recovery from every possible failure.
completion_criteria.label: Deep-space performance established within tested conditions and operational limits

related_concepts.text: Roster-based synthesis: AER-01, Mass-access orbital transportation, concerns moving people and cargo to orbit; AER-04 concerns sustaining people after arrival and during extended travel. Cheaper transportation could ease supply logistics, while near-closed life support could reduce the amount of recurring cargo required. AER-03, Industrial production of spacecraft propellant from extraterrestrial resources, similarly reduces dependence on Earth-supplied material, but its target is propulsion supply. Propellant production would not by itself demonstrate a functioning habitat’s air, water, food or maintenance cycles.

Roster-based synthesis: AER-06, General-purpose robotic construction of very large space systems, could overlap through habitat construction, maintenance and replacement manufacturing. Its defining achievement remains robotic construction rather than sustained human life support. AER-05, Economically competitive space-to-Earth solar power, concerns delivering power to terrestrial customers. Energy is an enabling input for a habitat, but commercial power delivery to Earth and material recycling for a crew require distinct demonstrations.

Roster-based synthesis: AER-02, A probe that returns data from another star system, shares the challenge of long-duration autonomous operation, but an uncrewed probe need not sustain human metabolism or nutrition. AER-08, A space observatory that can test for life on Earth-like exoplanets, concerns remote observation and scientific inference. AER-07, An operational defense against civilization-threatening asteroid impacts, concerns planetary defense. These capabilities may share space infrastructure or reliability methods with AER-04, but their completion would not establish near-closed human habitation.

Roster-based synthesis: AER-09, Sustained, useful air-breathing hypersonic flight, and AER-10, Fossil-fuel-free electric propulsion for large, long-range passenger aircraft, address atmospheric flight and propulsion. They share broad concerns about efficiency, thermal management and dependable operation, but neither directly tests the multi-year material cycles, nutrition or repair budgets central to AER-04. Each remains a separate innovation.

unresolved_issues: The supplied material does not define numerical limits for acceptable external inputs, inventory depletion or practical resource budgets.
Crew size, exact test duration, system architecture, nutritional assessment methods and representative failure scenarios remain unspecified.
The retained article cannot establish whether the approximately 98% wording appeared in its original December 10, 2025 version.
The empty bounded search record prevents determining whether later or other relevant demonstrations change the picture through November 1, 2026.

The complete proposed integration requirements and their feasibility are not established by the single supplied source; they remain engineering synthesis rather than documented whole-system achievements.

brief.title: Living for years in deep space with few deliveries
possible: Astronauts could spend years far from Earth with very few deliveries of supplies. Their habitat would reuse air, water and essential materials, provide food, and support repairs while keeping the crew healthy.
why: Long voyages would depend less on cargo sent from Earth. Crews could explore farther away, and remote outposts could stay occupied through longer gaps between deliveries.

sources.showed: Space station systems recycle wastewater, clean cabin air and generate oxygen. Crews also tested making tools and parts in orbit.
sources.quote: The water processor reclaims wastewater from crew members’ urine, cabin humidity, and the hydration systems inside spacesuits for spacewalks, converting it into clean, drinkable water.
sources.cited_for: Working air and water recycling provides a foundation for missions with little resupply.
sources.not_established: These systems do not establish years of operation with food, nutrients, supplies and repairs all within a small delivery budget.

sources.who: B. G. Bugbee and F. B. Salisbury, Utah State University
sources.showed: Controlled wheat-growing trials found that grain yields rose almost linearly as plants received more light.
sources.quote: Results indicate that an increase in the percentage of absorbed photons is responsible for most of the improvement in wheat yields in an optimal controlled environment.
sources.cited_for: Controlled crop production supports the food-growing part of life support.
sources.not_established: Crop yields alone do not establish a complete diet or a habitat that recycles nutrients and manages waste for years.

sources.who: Jianlou Yang, Yuming Fu and Hong Liu, Beihang University
sources.showed: In the ground-based Lunar Palace habitat, crew changes altered the mix of airborne bacteria. Researchers observed no differences in microbial function or antibiotic resistance.
sources.quote: We found that the bacterial community diversity in the Lunar Palace1 (LP1) system was higher than that in a controlled environment but lower than that in an open environment.
sources.cited_for: An inhabited habitat experiment provides findings on airborne microbes during prolonged confinement.
sources.not_established: Microbial measurements do not establish complete nutrition, material recycling or recovery from equipment failures in deep space.

shown: NASA reports that the International Space Station can recover around 98% of the water brought aboard. The station still depends on deliveries.

Beihang University's Lunar Palace experiment lasted 370 days on Earth with rotating crews. Its habitat combined plant growing, animal protein production, nutrient recovery from urine and processing of solid waste.
missing: A crewed test lasting several years still needs to account independently for all supplies, recovered materials and depleted stores.
The whole system still needs to sustain safe air, water and nutrition while repairing realistic failures within its resource budgets.
An integrated system still needs to demonstrate dependable operation in deep space with restricted deliveries and outside help.

milestones.label: Years of habitation with all material flows accounted for
milestones.explanation: A crewed test lasting several years would have to measure all material inputs, losses and changes in stored supplies against predefined limits. This would reveal how much the habitat depends on deliveries and reserves.

milestones.label: Healthy living and repairs within resource budgets
milestones.explanation: The test would have to sustain safe living conditions and nutrition while handling realistic failures within budgets for repair supplies, energy and crew effort. This would establish whether recycling remains dependable when equipment fails.

milestones.label: Dependable operation under tested deep-space conditions
milestones.explanation: A deep-space trial would have to establish performance under the conditions and limits on outside support it encounters. This would define the crew, duration, power and failure conditions within which the system can work.

uncertain: Acceptable limits for deliveries, depletion of stored supplies and total resource use remain undefined.
Crew size, test duration, nutrition measures and representative equipment failures remain to be specified.
Small recycling losses and repair demands may accumulate beyond practical mission budgets over several years.

page.title: Regenerative life support for multi-year deep-space missions
page.definition: An integrated system sustains a crew beyond low Earth orbit for more than 800 days without resupply, recycling wastewater and recovering oxygen from exhaled carbon dioxide. It supports onboard diagnosis and repair; food, consumables and spares may be stocked before departure.

goal.need: NASA's planning baseline assigns approximately 21,700 kg to food and spares for four crew over 860 days, with a 0.99 probability of sufficient supplies. Its ISS operational baseline assumes resupply every 2–6 months. Regeneration reduces consumable replacement, while onboard maintenance addresses dependence on replacement hardware.

figures.caption: NASA's 2023 food-and-spares planning baseline.
figures.note: A planning baseline using ISS capabilities, not measurements from a completed Mars mission.

statements.body: NASA, Next Generation Life Support programme
statements.quote: For a long duration exploration mission to be truly autonomous, growing food in situ will be necessary.
statements.context: The passage concerns bioregenerative life support, which uses organisms to regenerate resources. The page was updated on 22 June 2026.

statements.quote: the ultimate goal of recycling carbon dioxide, water and organic waste into food, water and oxygen.
statements.context: MELiSSA develops biological and physicochemical processes for regenerative life support.

completion.title: A crew completes more than 800 days of Mars transit without life-support resupply.
completion.criterion: An integrated regenerative life-support system sustains a crew through a single Mars-transit mission lasting more than 800 days without resupply. It provides Earth-independent diagnostics and repair and meets NASA's accompanying targets: more than 98% water recovery and more than 75% oxygen recovery at a cabin carbon dioxide partial pressure of 2 mmHg. Initial stocks of food, consumables and replacement hardware are permitted; the target specifies no crew size or total initial inventory.
completion.set_by: NASA, Advanced Habitation Systems Overview, 19 September 2023, slide 6, Life Support capability targets.
completion.threshold_quote: Enable single missions >800 days w/o resupply (T)
completion.basis: NASA explicitly identifies duration, absence of resupply, recovery targets and onboard repair for transit to Mars. These define a finite mission capability; they do not establish complete food recycling or a total-material closure percentage.

milestones.title: Four people complete 90 days with integrated biological and physicochemical life support.
milestones.criterion: Complete NASA's Phase III objective: a 90-day ground test with four human subjects and integrated biological and physicochemical life support. The 1997 experiment ran for 91 days, regenerating air and water and processing waste. Wheat supplied approximately 25% of crew oxygen demand; crops supplied less than 5% of caloric requirements. These results establish integration, not food self-sufficiency.
milestones.set_by: NASA, Lunar-Mars Life Support Test Project Phase III test objective, published in NASA/TM-1998-207911.
milestones.threshold_quote: a 90-day regenerative life support system test involving four human subjects to demonstrate an integrated biological and physiochemical life support system.

milestones.title: Spacecraft life-support hardware demonstrates approximately 98% overall water recovery.
milestones.criterion: Demonstrate overall water recovery close to 98%, including recovery from urine brine and cabin humidity. NASA reported achievement aboard ISS on 20 June 2023; its later station-technology account also reports around 98%. These are agency reports, not peer-reviewed results. Neither account specifies the demonstration duration or crew sample size. The percentage concerns water recovery, not total life-support closure.
milestones.set_by: NASA, NASA Achieves Water Recovery Milestone on International Space Station, 20 June 2023.
milestones.threshold_quote: life support systems need to recover close to 98% of the water

milestones.title: A life-support system recovers more than 75% of oxygen at 2 mmHg cabin carbon dioxide.
milestones.criterion: Recover more than 75% of oxygen from metabolic carbon dioxide while operating at a cabin carbon dioxide partial pressure of 2 mmHg. NASA's presentation dated 17 August 2023 gives an ISS baseline of approximately 47% under that carbon dioxide condition. It specifies no acceptance-test duration or sample size for the target.
milestones.set_by: NASA, ECLSS-CHP System Capability Leadership Team overview, 17 August 2023, slide 18; target written for transit to Mars.

milestones.title: An integrated life-support ground test including humans exceeds three years of operation.
milestones.criterion: Operate an integrated life-support system in a ground test including humans for more than three years, demonstrating long-duration performance and reliability before deployment beyond low Earth orbit. NASA specifies no fixed crew size or recovery percentages for this test. A shorter related demonstration, Lunar Palace 365, lasted 370 days from 10 May 2017 to 15 May 2018, with eight volunteers rotating in four-person crews; it does not meet this duration.
milestones.set_by: NASA Thermal/ECLSS Steering Committee, Environmental Control and Life Support Integrated Roadmap Development, Mission 2 strategy, page 29.
milestones.threshold_quote: testing should exceed three years of run time at minimum

not_found: No single total-material closure threshold covering food, nutrients, consumables and replacement hardware was found in NASA roadmaps or ESA MELiSSA goals.
No published acceptance protocol specifying crew size, inventory limits and failure-recovery criteria for NASA's more-than-800-day target was found.
No qualifying flight result above 75% oxygen recovery at 2 mmHg cabin carbon dioxide was found.
No opened source documents an integrated human ground test exceeding three years or a crewed Mars-transit mission exceeding 800 days without resupply.
The supplied 1991 NASA PDF could not be opened after repeated fetch timeouts.

results.finding: ISS life-support systems recover around 98% of water; crew sample size not stated.
results.detail: The article identifies urine and cabin humidity as water sources but does not specify the demonstration duration or crew sample size.
results.quote: can recover around 98% of the water brought to the station

results.finding: Lunar Palace 365 operated for 370 days with eight volunteers in rotating crews.
results.detail: The integrated ground test fell short of the more-than-three-year duration.
results.quote: A total of eight volunteers were divided into two groups (G1 and G2; 2 females and 2 males each) that spent a total of 370 days in the LP1.

results.finding: NASA's Phase III integrated life support test supported four crew members for 91 days.
results.detail: The test integrated biological and physical-chemical systems for air, water and solid waste recovery. The abstract does not quantify the crops' contribution to oxygen or calories.
results.quote: The Phase III test broke new ground for the U.S. Space Program by being the first test to look at integration of biological and physical-chemical systems for air, water and solid waste recovery for a crew of four for 91 days.

results.finding: NASA Phase III: four crew members completed 91 days with integrated biological and physicochemical life support.
results.detail: Wheat supplied oxygen equivalent to one crew member’s demand and less than 5% of the crew’s caloric intake. Water was recycled, and fecal waste was processed.
results.quote:
The final test was the Phase III test, which incorporated the use of 
biological systems in concert with physicochemical (P/C) life support 
system technologies to continuously recycle air, water, and part of the 
solid waste stream generated by a 4-person crew for 91 days.

results.finding: ISS water recovery system: 99% total water recovery; crew sample size not specified.
results.detail: NASA reports 19 brine-processing operations by February 2023. The combined system processed urine brine and cabin humidity; the demonstration duration is not specified.
results.quote: The results demonstrated that 99% total water recovery from UPA, WPA, and BPA was achieved.

results.finding: ISS brine processor: approximately 98% water recovery; crew sample size not specified.
results.detail: The paper describes recovery from urine brine through the cabin humidity system, but does not clearly establish that 98% is overall water recovery. It separately describes 97–98% as an early estimate for urine recovery.
results.quote:
The BPA operate s on ISS as a Technology 
Demonstration for NASA Exploration missions  and processes the brine generated by the UPA to remove water and 
thereby achieving ~98% water recovery.

results.finding: Biosphere 2 Mission One sustained eight crew members in a closed life-support facility for 2 years.
results.detail: The ground test fell short of the required more than three years. Oxygen was added during the closure after atmospheric levels declined.
results.quote:
Mission one was the ﬁrst experimental closure
of Biosphere 2 with eight crew members for 2 years, 1991–1993.
